title: Linked Lists from Scratch
summary: A **linked list** stores each element in its own node, and each node points to the next. Inserting and removing anywhere is cheap, but finding anything means following pointers one at a time. Building one by hand is the best practice there is for pointers, and it explains why games use them rarely and carefully.
markdown:
## Nodes and links An array keeps its elements side by side. A linked list scatters them: each element sits in a separately allocated **node**, together with a pointer to the next node. The list itself only remembers the first node, the **head**. ```cpp struct Node { int value; Node* next; // nullptr in the last node }; ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR H["head"] --> A["value 7
next"] A --> B["value 3
next"] B --> C["value 9
next = nullptr"] ``` Walking the list means following `next` until it is null: ```cpp #include struct Node { int value; Node* next; }; int main() { Node c{ 9, nullptr }; Node b{ 3, &c }; Node a{ 7, &b }; Node* head{ &a }; for (Node* n{ head }; n != nullptr; n = n->next) std::cout << n->value << ' '; std::cout << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ``` 7 3 9 ``` ## Inserting Adding at the front takes a constant amount of work, however long the list is: make a node, point it at the old head, make it the new head. ```cpp void pushFront(Node*& head, int value) { head = new Node{ value, head }; } ``` Inserting after a node you already have is just as cheap: two pointer writes, no elements moved. Compare an array, where inserting at the front means shifting every element along by one. ## Removing, and the pointer-to-pointer trick Removing a node means making whatever pointed at it point at its successor instead. The first node is pointed at by `head`; every other node is pointed at by the previous node's `next`. Treating those two cases separately is clumsy: ```cpp // Clumsy: a special case for the head. void removeFirstClumsy(Node*& head, int value) { if (head && head->value == value) { Node* dead{ head }; head = head->next; delete dead; return; } for (Node* n{ head }; n && n->next; n = n->next) if (n->next->value == value) { Node* dead{ n->next }; n->next = dead->next; delete dead; return; } } ``` The neat way is to walk with a **pointer to the link** itself, a `Node**` (lesson 3.01). It starts at `&head` and moves to `&node->next`. Whichever link it holds, removing the node it points at is the same one line: ```cpp void removeFirst(Node*& head, int value) { for (Node** link{ &head }; *link != nullptr; link = &(*link)->next) { if ((*link)->value == value) { Node* dead{ *link }; *link = dead->next; // whoever pointed at dead now skips it delete dead; return; } } } ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR H["head"] --> A["7"] A -->|"link points at this next"| B["3 (dead)"] B --> C["9"] A -.->|"*link = dead->next"| C ``` This is one of the few places where `**` makes code shorter and clearer, and it is a classic interview question. The practice task asks you to write it. ## The cost: walking is slow | Operation | Array / `std::vector` | Linked list | |---|---|---| | Get element number `i` | One calculation | Follow `i` pointers | | Insert or remove at the front | Move every element | Two pointer writes | | Insert or remove in the middle, given its position | Move the elements after it | Two pointer writes | | Loop over everything | Walks memory in order | Jumps around the heap: one cache miss per node, likely | | Extra memory | None | One pointer (8 bytes) per element, plus allocator overhead | That last-but-one row usually decides it. Looping over a `std::vector` of a million elements reads contiguous memory the processor can stream in. Looping over a list of a million nodes follows a million dependent pointers into scattered heap blocks (lesson 3.02's pointer chasing). In practice the vector is often ten times faster or more, even for workloads with many inserts, because shifting contiguous memory is so cheap. So the standard advice is: **default to `std::vector`**. Use a list only when you have measured a reason. ## Where lists do appear in games - **Intrusive lists**: the `next` pointer lives inside an object that already exists for another reason, such as all the enemies in one grid cell of a spatial partition. No extra allocations, and an object can unlink itself in constant time. - **Free lists** in pools (lesson 3.10): unused slots point to the next unused slot, so allocating is "take the head". - **Engines' own systems**, such as lists of timers or render commands, often allocated from an arena so the nodes are close together anyway. The standard library has `std::list` (doubly linked) and `std::forward_list` (singly linked) if you need one. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Using a node after deleting it > In `n = n->next` after `delete n`, the read is from freed memory. Save `next` first. > [!warning] Losing the rest of the list > Overwriting `head` before saving the old head leaks every node. Draw the arrows before writing the code. > [!warning] Forgetting to free the nodes > A list built with `new` needs a loop that deletes every node, or nodes owned by `std::unique_ptr`. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does each node of a singly linked list hold? + An element's value and a pointer to the next node, or `nullptr` in the last node - Only a pointer to the next node - An element's value and pointers to both the next and the previous node > Pointers in both directions make a doubly linked list. A singly linked list only links forward. ? Why is inserting at the front of a list cheap? - Because the list keeps spare nodes ready + Because it creates one node and changes two pointers, whatever the list's length - Because the new node is placed next to the old first node in memory - Because nodes are never freed > Nothing has to move, unlike inserting at the front of a vector, which shifts every element. ? Give two situations where games use linked structures sensibly. - Storing all game objects for a fast loop, and storing tile maps + Intrusive lists inside existing objects, and pool free lists - Replacing every `std::vector`, and holding strings - Sorting large arrays, and looking up items by name > Lists are slow to walk, so they appear where links are cheap to keep and walking is rare or short. An intrusive list keeps the link inside objects that already exist, such as the objects in one grid cell. ? What is the cost of reading the 1000th element of a linked list? - One memory read + Following 999 `next` pointers from the head - Sorting the list first > There is no index arithmetic: the only way to a node is through the ones before it. ? In `removeFirst`, why does `link` have type `Node**`? - Because nodes are stored in a two-dimensional array - To make the function faster + It points at the link (`head` or a `next`) that may change > Changing a pointer requires its address. `*link = dead->next` updates whichever pointer pointed at the dead node. ? Why is a `std::vector` usually faster to loop over than a linked list with the same elements? + Its elements are contiguous and cache-friendly; list nodes are scattered - Vectors use less memory per element because they compress values - Linked lists must be sorted > Contiguous memory is streamed efficiently; pointer chasing waits on memory at every step. ```
ideas:
- Write `pushBack(head, value)` that walks to the last node and attaches a new one. How does its cost grow with the length of the list?
- Draw the arrows on paper for `removeFirst(head, 7)` where 7 is the head, then for 9 where 9 is the last node. Check that the one line handles both.
- Pause a program with a list in the Visual Studio debugger and expand `head` repeatedly through `next`.

cards.q: What does each node of a singly linked list hold?
cards.a:
An element's value and a pointer to the next node, or `nullptr` in the last node

Pointers in both directions make a doubly linked list. A singly linked list only links forward.

cards.q: Why is inserting at the front of a list cheap?
cards.a:
Because it creates one node and changes two pointers, whatever the list's length

Nothing has to move, unlike inserting at the front of a vector, which shifts every element.

cards.q: Give two situations where games use linked structures sensibly.
cards.a:
Intrusive lists inside existing objects, and pool free lists

Lists are slow to walk, so they appear where links are cheap to keep and walking is rare or short. An intrusive list keeps the link inside objects that already exist, such as the objects in one grid cell.

cards.q: What is the cost of reading the 1000th element of a linked list?
cards.a:
Following 999 `next` pointers from the head

There is no index arithmetic: the only way to a node is through the ones before it.

It points at the link (`head` or a `next`) that may change

Changing a pointer requires its address. `*link = dead->next` updates whichever pointer pointed at the dead node.

cards.q: Why is a `std::vector` usually faster to loop over than a linked list with the same elements?
cards.a:
Its elements are contiguous and cache-friendly; list nodes are scattered

Contiguous memory is streamed efficiently; pointer chasing waits on memory at every step.
